claim: Fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) is a tumor cell survival factor that is transported into the extracellular space by an unconventional secretory mechanism.
source: Fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) is a tumor cell survival factor that is transported into the extracellular space by an unconventional secretory mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript regarding FGF2's role and secretion mechanism.

claim: Cell surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans play an essential role in unconventional secretion of FGF2.
source: Cell surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans are known to play an essential role in this process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior research cited in the introduction.

claim: Glypican-1 (GPC1) is the principle and rate-limiting factor that drives unconventional secretion of FGF2.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that among the diverse subclasses consisting of syndecans, perlecans, glypicans, and others, Glypican-1 (GPC1) is the principle and rate-limiting factor that drives unconventional secretion of FGF2.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including BioID screen, knockout studies, and secretion assays shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: GPC1 is dispensable for FGF2 signaling into cells.
source: By contrast, we demonstrate GPC1 to be dispensable for FGF2 signaling into cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ERK1/2 phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: Disaccharides with N-linked sulfate groups are enriched in the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1.
source: We provide first insights into the structural basis for GPC1-dependent FGF2 secretion, identifying disaccharides with N-linked sulfate groups to be enriched in the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 to which FGF2 binds with high affinity.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis of disaccharide composition shown in Figure 7.

claim: FGF2 binds to GPC1 with high affinity.
source: identifying disaccharides with N-linked sulfate groups to be enriched in the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 to which FGF2 binds with high affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biolayer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: GPC1 was identified as the strongest hit in a BioID screen for proteins in proximity to FGF2.
source: The strongest hit of this screen was GPC1, a GPI-anchored HSPG associated with cell surfaces (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plot in Figure 1D from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: GPC1 knockout severely impairs FGF2 secretion in HeLa cells.
source: These experiments revealed a strong decrease in FGF2 secretion efficiency when GPC1 was absent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell surface biotinylation and flow cytometry assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: GPC5 knockout does not impact FGF2 secretion.
source: By contrast, a knockout of GPC5 did not impact this process.
evidence: This is shown in the secretion assays in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of GPC1 increases FGF2 secretion efficiency above wild-type levels.
source: In all cell lines described, overexpression of GPC1 did not only rescue the knockout of the endogenous GPC1 gene but rather increased the efficiency of FGF2 secretion to levels well above HeLa wild-type cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the secretion assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: GPC1 knockout cells contain normal amounts of total glycosaminoglycans.
source: Even though HeLa cell lines lacking GPC1 were found to contain normal amounts of total glycosaminoglycans, FGF2 secretion was severely impaired.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification of total GAG chains in Figure 3B.

claim: GPC1 knockout cells have normal amounts of total heparan sulfate chains.
source: there were no significant differences in the total amounts of both glycosaminoglycan chains (Figure 3B) and heparan sulfate chains (Figure 3C) in all engineered cell lines analyzed in comparison to HeLa wild-type cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GPC1 overexpression increases FGF2-GFP binding capacity to cell surfaces.
source: Strikingly, all types of cell lines overexpressing GPC1 were characterized by significantly increased binding capacities for FGF2-GFP.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: GPC5 overexpression does not increase FGF2-GFP binding to cell surfaces.
source: Again, GPC5 overexpression did not result in increased binding of FGF2-GFP to cell surfaces (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the flow cytometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: GPC2, GPC4, and GPC6 can rescue FGF2 secretion in GPC1 knockout cells.
source: By contrast, all GPCs belonging to the GPC1 subfamily rescued FGF2 secretion in a GPC1 knockout background. While GPC2 and GPC4 did so at the level of HeLa wild-type cells, GPC6 overexpression increased the efficiency of FGF2 secretion above HeLa wild-type levels.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 4.

claim: GPC3 and GPC5 cannot rescue FGF2 secretion in GPC1 knockout cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and C, like GPC5, GPC3 was incapable of promoting efficient FGF2 secretion in the absence of GPC1.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: SDC4 overexpression does not rescue FGF2 secretion in GPC1 knockout cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4D and E, SDC4 overexpression neither rescued FGF2 secretion nor did it affect the cell surface binding capacities for recombinant FGF2-GFP.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 4D and E.

claim: A GPC1 variant with a transmembrane domain instead of a GPI anchor is functional in supporting FGF2 secretion.
source: This was particularly evident from the fact that an engineered version of GPC1 in which the GPI anchor was replaced by a membrane span ('GPC1 TM') was functional in GPC1 knockout cells, both with regard to supporting efficient secretion of FGF2 (Figure 4D) and cell surface binding capacities for recombinant FGF2-GFP (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: GPC1 overexpression increases the number of FGF2-GFP particles on cell surfaces by about 50% at high FGF2-GFP expression levels.
source: When cells were analyzed expressing FGF2-GFP at high levels, the average number of FGF2-GFP particles on cell surfaces was increased by about 50% in a pool of GPC1-overexpressing cells relative to CHO wild-type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by single molecule TIRF microscopy in Figure 5B.

claim: GPC1 overexpression increases the number of FGF2-GFP particles on cell surfaces by more than fourfold at low FGF2-GFP expression levels.
source: This difference was even more pronounced in cells expressing low levels of FGF2-GFP resulting in a more than fourfold higher average number of FGF2-GFP particles on the cell surfaces of GPC1-overexpressing cells compared to wild-type cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by single molecule TIRF microscopy in Figure 5D.

claim: FGF2 binds to GPC1 at concentrations as low as 0.8 nM.
source: It revealed a strong interaction of FGF2 with GPC1 that was detectable already at the lowest FGF2 concentration being used at 0.8 nM (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6A.

claim: GPC5 shows only weak interactions with FGF2 even at 60 nM concentration.
source: By contrast, even at the highest concentration of FGF2 (60 nM), GPC5 only showed weak interactions with FGF2 (Figure 5C) that were barely above the levels of the negative controls, GPC1-ΔHS (Figure 6B) or heparan sulfate binding mutants of FGF2 tested against GPC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6C.

claim: GPC6 displays significant FGF2 binding capabilities, but less efficiently than GPC1.
source: Unlike GPC5, GPC6, a member of the GPC1 sub-family of GPCs that was capable of rescuing a GPC1 knockout (Figure 4A and B), displayed significant binding capabilities of FGF2, however, less efficiently compared to GPC1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6D.

claim: SDC4 shows weak interactions with FGF2 at concentrations up to 60 nM.
source: Finally, similar to GPC5, SDC4, a member of the SDC family of proteoglycans, showed weak interactions with FGF2 at concentrations of up to 60 nM (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6E.

claim: GPC1 exhibits only weak or no interactions with EGF and IFNγ.
source: As documented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, beyond further controls using heparan sulfate binding mutants of FGF2, we found GPC1 to exhibit only weak or no interactions with other examples of growth factors or cytokines such as EGF and IFNγ.
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Galectin-1 and galectin-3 are not capable of interacting with GPC1.
source: Similarly, examples for other extracellular proteins secreted by unconventional means such as galectin-1 and galectin-3 (Rabouille, 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018; Pallotta and Nickel, 2020) were observed not to be capable of interacting with GPC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by biolayer interferometry in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Disaccharides corresponding to standards 1, 2, and 5 (containing N-linked sulfates) are enriched in GPC1 over GPC5.
source: This analysis revealed the enrichment of disaccharides in GPC1 over GPC5 that correspond to the disaccharide standards 1, 2, and 5. All of these disaccharides contain N-linked sulfates (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by HPLC analysis of disaccharide composition in Figure 7B.

claim: Disaccharide standard 1 (a tri-sulfated disaccharide) shows the biggest difference in abundance between GPC1 and GPC5.
source: The biggest difference between GPC1 and GPC5 was found to be the disaccharide standard 1 that represents a tri-sulfated disaccharide with two O-linked and one N-linked sulfate group.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: The FGF2 binding site in co-crystals contains three disaccharides of the type represented by disaccharide standard 1.
source: Intriguingly, when FGF2 was co-crystallized with synthetic heparin molecules, the binding site was found to contain three disaccharides of the type represented by the disaccharide standard 1 (Raman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from a structural study by Raman et al., 2003.

claim: Disaccharides lacking both O- and N-linked sulfations (standards 6 and 12) are more abundant in GPC5 compared to GPC1.
source: By contrast, disaccharides lacking both O- and N-linked sulfations corresponding to the disaccharide standards 6 and 12 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) were more abundant in GPC5 compared to GPC1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: GPC1 knockout, GPC1 overexpression, and wild-type cells show similar levels of ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to FGF2.
source: At both 10 and 1 ng/ml FGF2, all types of cells indicated showed reduced FGF2 signaling when treated with heparinases (Figure 8A [quantification with statistics] and Figure 8B [representative Western analysis of ERK phosphorylation]). By contrast, neither a knockout nor overexpression of GPC1 had any significant impact on phosphorylated ERK1/2 levels at both 10 and 1 ng/ml FGF2 added to cells (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is shown by ERK1/2 phosphorylation assays in Figure 8.

claim: Heparinase treatment reduces FGF2 signaling in all cell types tested.
source: At both 10 and 1 ng/ml FGF2, all types of cells indicated showed reduced FGF2 signaling when treated with heparinases (Figure 8A [quantification with statistics] and Figure 8B [representative Western analysis of ERK phosphorylation]).
evidence: This is shown by ERK1/2 phosphorylation assays in Figure 8.

claim: Heparan sulfates are characterized by about 20–300 negatively charged residues with structural modifications such as epimerization and sulfation patterns.
source: Heparan sulfates are characterized by about 20–300 negatively charged residues with almost infinite structural modifications such as epimerization and sulfation patterns that are dynamically processed by enzymes resulting in variations between tissues, developmental stages, and the type of core protein they are attached to (Turnbull et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Turnbull et al., 2001.

claim: Glypicans contain a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor.
source: Different classes of HSPGs also differ in terms of how they are anchored to membranes in that glypicans (GPCs) contain a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor whereas syndecans (SDCs) carry transmembrane spans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HSPG structure.

claim: Syndecans carry transmembrane spans.
source: Different classes of HSPGs also differ in terms of how they are anchored to membranes in that glypicans (GPCs) contain a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor whereas syndecans (SDCs) carry transmembrane spans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HSPG structure.

claim: GPCs and SDCs partition into liquid ordered and disordered domains, respectively.
source: Based on their differential modes of membrane association, GPCs and SDCs partition into liquid ordered and disordered domains, respectively, providing a structural basis for distinct roles in growth factor signaling (Gutiérrez and Brandan, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gutiérrez and Brandan, 2010.

claim: FGF2 is a pro-angiogenic factor involved in cell proliferation and differentiation during development.
source: Among the proteins that bind to the alternating negatively charged disaccharide units of heparan sulfate chains in HSPGs is fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) (Lindahl et al., 1999; Murphy et al., 2004), a pro-angiogenic factor involved in cell proliferation and differentiation during development.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lindahl et al., 1999 and Murphy et al., 2004.

claim: FGF2 has a strong impact on tumor-induced angiogenesis under pathophysiological conditions.
source: In addition, under pathophysiological conditions, FGF2 has a strong impact on tumor-induced angiogenesis triggering the formation of new blood vessels to provide the large demands of malignant cancers for nutrients and oxygen (Carmeliet, 2000; Akl et al., 2015; Akl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Carmeliet, 2000; Akl et al., 2015; Akl et al., 2016.

claim: FGF2 plays a critical role as a tumor cell survival factor blocking programmed cell death through both autocrine and paracrine signaling.
source: FGF2 also plays a critical role as a tumor cell survival factor blocking programmed cell death through both autocrine and paracrine signaling (Okada-Ban et al., 2000; Akl et al., 2016; Traer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Okada-Ban et al., 2000; Akl et al., 2016; Traer et al., 2016.

claim: FGF2 lacks a signal peptide and does not have access to the ER/Golgi-dependent secretory pathway.
source: While the majority of extracellular proteins contain N-terminal signal peptides for ER-Golgi-dependent protein secretion (Palade, 1975; Rothman, 1994; Rothman and Wieland, 1996; Schekman and Orci, 1996), FGF2 lacks a signal peptide and thus does not have access to the ER/Golgi-dependent secretory pathway (Nickel, 2005; Nickel, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Nickel, 2005; Nickel, 2007.

claim: FGF2 is secreted by an unconventional mechanism based on direct protein translocation across the plasma membrane (UPS Type I).
source: The mechanism by which FGF2 is transported into the extracellular space is based on direct protein translocation across the plasma membrane (UPS Type I) (Schäfer et al., 2004; Zehe et al., 2006; Rabouille, 2017; Steringer et al., 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018; Dimou et al., 2019; Pallotta and Nickel, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations describing the mechanism.

claim: The Na,K-ATPase plays a role in unconventional secretion of FGF2.
source: All molecular components known to date to play a role in unconventional secretion of FGF2 are physically associated with the plasma membrane. These factors include the Na,K-ATPase (Zacherl et al., 2015), Tec kinase which is recruited to the inner leaflet via binding to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Ebert et al., 2010; Steringer et al., 2012; La Venuta et al., 2016), and PI(4,5)P2 (Temmerman et al., 2008; Temmerman and Nickel, 2009; Nickel, 2011), the most abundant phosphoinositide at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zacherl et al., 2015.

claim: Tec kinase plays a role in unconventional secretion of FGF2 and is recruited to the inner leaflet via binding to PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: These factors include the Na,K-ATPase (Zacherl et al., 2015), Tec kinase which is recruited to the inner leaflet via binding to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Ebert et al., 2010; Steringer et al., 2012; La Venuta et al., 2016), and PI(4,5)P2 (Temmerman et al., 2008; Temmerman and Nickel, 2009; Nickel, 2011), the most abundant phosphoinositide at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Ebert et al., 2010; Steringer et al., 2012; La Venuta et al., 2016.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 plays a role in unconventional secretion of FGF2.
source: These factors include the Na,K-ATPase (Zacherl et al., 2015), Tec kinase which is recruited to the inner leaflet via binding to PI(3,4,5)P3 (Ebert et al., 2010; Steringer et al., 2012; La Venuta et al., 2016), and PI(4,5)P2 (Temmerman et al., 2008; Temmerman and Nickel, 2009; Nickel, 2011), the most abundant phosphoinositide at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Temmerman et al., 2008; Temmerman and Nickel, 2009; Nickel, 2011.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is the most abundant phosphoinositide at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: and PI(4,5)P2 (Temmerman et al., 2008; Temmerman and Nickel, 2009; Nickel, 2011), the most abundant phosphoinositide at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006.

claim: The Na,K-ATPase is the first contact for FGF2 at the inner plasma membrane leaflet.
source: In the above-mentioned studies, FGF2 has been demonstrated to engage in direct physical interactions with all three of these components with the Na,K-ATPase being the first contact for FGF2 at the inner plasma membrane leaflet (Legrand et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Legrand et al., 2020.

claim: FGF2 interacts with PI(4,5)P2 through a cluster of basic amino acids (K127, R128, and K133).
source: Through subsequent interactions with PI(4,5)P2 mediated by a cluster of basic amino acids on the molecular surface of FGF2 (K127, R128, and K133 [Temmerman et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2015; Steringer et al., 2017]), the core mechanism of FGF2 membrane translocation is triggered.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Temmerman et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2015; Steringer et al., 2017.

claim: FGF2 membrane translocation involves membrane insertion of FGF2 oligomers.
source: This process involves membrane insertion of FGF2 oligomers (Steringer et al., 2012; Steringer et al., 2017; Steringer and Nickel, 2018) whose biogenesis depends on two surface cysteines in FGF2 that drive oligomerization through the formation of intermolecular disulfide bridges (Müller et al., 2015; Steringer et al., 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Steringer et al., 2012; Steringer et al., 2017; Steringer and Nickel, 2018.

claim: FGF2 oligomerization depends on two surface cysteines that form intermolecular disulfide bridges.
source: This process involves membrane insertion of FGF2 oligomers (Steringer et al., 2012; Steringer et al., 2017; Steringer and Nickel, 2018) whose biogenesis depends on two surface cysteines in FGF2 that drive oligomerization through the formation of intermolecular disulfide bridges (Müller et al., 2015; Steringer et al., 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Müller et al., 2015; Steringer et al., 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018.

claim: Membrane-inserted FGF2 oligomers are accommodated within a lipidic membrane pore with a toroidal architecture.
source: Membrane-inserted FGF2 oligomers are accommodated within a lipidic membrane pore with a toroidal architecture (Steringer et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2015; Steringer and Nickel, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Steringer et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2015; Steringer and Nickel, 2018.

claim: Heparan sulfates have an about 100-fold higher affinity for FGF2 compared to PI(4,5)P2.
source: A critical property of heparan sulfates for this function is their ability to out-compete PI(4,5)P2 with regard to physical interactions toward FGF2. These are mutually exclusive with heparan sulfates having an about 100-fold higher affinity for FGF2 compared to PI(4,5)P2 (Steringer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Steringer et al., 2017.

claim: FGF2 on cell surfaces undergoes intercellular spreading by direct cell-cell contacts.
source: FGF2 on cell surfaces undergoes intercellular spreading by direct cell-cell contacts, probably mediated by direct exchange between heparan sulfate chains that are physically associated with opposing cell surfaces (Zehe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zehe et al., 2006.

claim: HSPGs mediate the final step of FGF2 secretion.
source: Thus, during the lifetime of an FGF2 molecule, the role of HSPGs is threefold with (i) mediating the final step of FGF2 secretion (Zehe et al., 2006; Nickel, 2007), (ii) protecting FGF2 on cell surfaces against degradation and denaturation (Nugent and Iozzo, 2000), and (iii) mediating FGF2 signaling as part of ternary complexes containing FGF2, heparan sulfate chains, and FGF high-affinity receptors (Presta et al., 2005; Ribatti et al., 2007; Belov and Mohammadi, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zehe et al., 2006; Nickel, 2007.

claim: HSPGs protect FGF2 on cell surfaces against degradation and denaturation.
source: Thus, during the lifetime of an FGF2 molecule, the role of HSPGs is threefold with (i) mediating the final step of FGF2 secretion (Zehe et al., 2006; Nickel, 2007), (ii) protecting FGF2 on cell surfaces against degradation and denaturation (Nugent and Iozzo, 2000), and (iii) mediating FGF2 signaling as part of ternary complexes containing FGF2, heparan sulfate chains, and FGF high-affinity receptors (Presta et al., 2005; Ribatti et al., 2007; Belov and Mohammadi, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Nugent and Iozzo, 2000.

claim: HSPGs mediate FGF2 signaling as part of ternary complexes containing FGF2, heparan sulfate chains, and FGF high-affinity receptors.
source: Thus, during the lifetime of an FGF2 molecule, the role of HSPGs is threefold with (i) mediating the final step of FGF2 secretion (Zehe et al., 2006; Nickel, 2007), (ii) protecting FGF2 on cell surfaces against degradation and denaturation (Nugent and Iozzo, 2000), and (iii) mediating FGF2 signaling as part of ternary complexes containing FGF2, heparan sulfate chains, and FGF high-affinity receptors (Presta et al., 2005; Ribatti et al., 2007; Belov and Mohammadi, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Presta et al., 2005; Ribatti et al., 2007; Belov and Mohammadi, 2013.

claim: FGF2 membrane translocation has been confirmed in a fully reconstituted system using giant unilamellar vesicles.
source: It has recently been confirmed in a fully reconstituted system using giant unilamellar vesicles (Steringer et al., 2017) and is consistent with earlier observations demonstrating that membrane translocation depends on a fully folded state of FGF2 that permits PI(4,5)P2-dependent FGF2 oligomerization and interactions with heparan sulfate chains (Backhaus et al., 2004; Torrado et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Steringer et al., 2017.

claim: FGF2 membrane translocation takes an average time interval of about 200 ms.
source: Furthermore, PI(4,5)P2- and heparan-sulfate-dependent translocation of FGF2 across the plasma membrane has also been visualized in living cells using single molecule TIRF microscopy. These studies revealed the real-time kinetics of this process with an average time interval for FGF2 membrane translocation of about 200 ms (Dimou et al., 2019; Pallotta and Nickel, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Dimou et al., 2019; Pallotta and Nickel, 2020.

claim: The half-life of the BirA-biotinyl-5'-AMP complex of the BirA* R188G mutant enzyme is in the range of 5 s.
source: The half-life of the BirA-biotinyl-5'-AMP complex of the BirA* R188G mutant enzyme used in our BioID screens is in the range of 5 s (Kwon and Beckett, 2000; Oostdyk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kwon and Beckett, 2000; Oostdyk et al., 2019.

claim: FGF2-GFP translocates across the plasma membrane within an average time interval of 200 ms.
source: By comparison, FGF2-GFP has been shown to translocate across the plasma membrane within an average time interval of 200 ms (Dimou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Dimou et al., 2019.

claim: Endocytosis of FGF2-GFP could not be detected in HeLa S3 wild-type, GPC1 knockout, or GPC1 knockout cells overexpressing GPC1 over a time course of 60 min.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and in the Videos 1–3, endocytosis of FGF2-GFP along a time course of 60 min could neither be detected in HeLa S3 wild-type, GPC1 knockout, nor in GPC1 knockout cells overexpressing GPC1.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy time-lapse imaging in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Videos 1-3.

claim: The observed differences in cell surface levels of FGF2 represent true FGF2 secretion phenotypes not compromised by increased rates of endocytosis in GPC1 knockout cells.
source: Therefore, the observed differences in the cell surface levels of FGF2 (Figure 2) represent true FGF2 secretion phenotypes that were not compromised by increased rates of endocytosis in GPC1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the endocytosis experiments showing no differences between cell types.

claim: GPC1 is already required for membrane insertion of FGF2 oligomers at the inner plasma membrane leaflet.
source: These findings have implications for the molecular mechanism by which GPC1 is functioning in this process. Beyond the role of cell surface heparan sulfate chains in capturing and disassembling FGF2 oligomers at the outer plasma membrane leaflet (Zehe et al., 2006; Nickel, 2007; Rabouille, 2017; Dimou and Nickel, 2018; Pallotta and Nickel, 2020), they further suggest that GPC1 is already required for membrane insertion of FGF2 oligomers, an upstream step that is initiated at the inner plasma membrane leaflet.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GPC1 is rate-limiting and affects secretion efficiency.

claim: The heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 are positioned in close proximity to its GPI anchor and the membrane surface.
source: Based upon the unique positioning of the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 in close proximity to its GPI anchor and therefore the membrane surface (Prydz and Dalen, 2000; Blackhall et al., 2001; Nakato and Kimata, 2002; De Pasquale and Pavone, 2020), the FGF2 binding sites in GPC1 appear to be required for stabilizing the first subunits of membrane-spanning FGF2 oligomers as they surface at the outer plasma membrane leaflet.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Prydz and Dalen, 2000; Blackhall et al., 2001; Nakato and Kimata, 2002; De Pasquale and Pavone, 2020.

claim: The heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 contain multiple copies of FGF2 hexasaccharide ligands in a clustered manner producing high avidity.
source: The strong interaction of GPC1 with FGF2 (Figure 6) therefore indicates that GPC1 carries heparan sulfate units consisting of three disaccharides corresponding to standard 1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) as identified in structural in vitro studies (Raman et al., 2003). In addition, the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 may contain multiple copies of these FGF2 hexasaccharide ligands in a clustered manner producing high avidity and, therefore, a strong apparent affinity toward FGF2.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the binding data and disaccharide composition analysis.

claim: GPC1 is not a general component of unconventional secretory processes.
source: These findings suggest that GPC1 is not a general component of unconventional secretory processes but may represent a highly specific molecular component driving FGF2 secretion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that galectin-1 and galectin-3 do not bind to GPC1.

claim: Other HSPGs such as SDCs are sufficient to support FGF2 signaling.
source: These findings suggest that other HSPGs such as SDCs are sufficient to support FGF2 signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GPC1 is dispensable for FGF2 signaling.

claim: Both FGF2 and GPC1 are key components of tumor progression for a wide range of cancer types.
source: Since both FGF2 and GPC1 are key components of tumor progression for a wide range of cancer types (Akl et al., 2016; Pan and Ho, 2021), we propose that the prominent function of GPC1 in driving efficient unconventional secretion of FGF2 might play a key role for tumor development such as acute myeloid leukemia (Traer et al., 2016; Javidi-Sharifi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Akl et al., 2016; Pan and Ho, 2021.

claim: The prominent function of GPC1 in driving efficient unconventional secretion of FGF2 might play a key role for tumor development such as acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Since both FGF2 and GPC1 are key components of tumor progression for a wide range of cancer types (Akl et al., 2016; Pan and Ho, 2021), we propose that the prominent function of GPC1 in driving efficient unconventional secretion of FGF2 might play a key role for tumor development such as acute myeloid leukemia (Traer et al., 2016; Javidi-Sharifi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is proposed as a speculation based on the findings and cited literature on tumor development.

claim: API5 is a known interaction partner of FGF2.
source: This analysis revealed known interaction partners of FGF2 such as API5 (Noh et al., 2014; Bong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Noh et al., 2014; Bong et al., 2020.

claim: FGF2 was identified in the BioID screen likely due to its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: In addition, FGF2 itself was identified likely due to its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the BioID screen results and known FGF2 oligomerization properties.

claim: The observed biotinylation of cell surface GPC1 mediated by FGF2-BirA* is consistent with the kinetic data on the stability of the BirA*-biotinyl-5'-AMP complex and the time interval for FGF2 translocation.
source: Therefore, the observed biotinylation of cell surface GPC1 mediated by FGF2-BirA* is consistent with the kinetic data on the stability of the BirA*-biotinyl-5'-AMP complex and the time interval it takes for FGF2 to translocate from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the half-life of the BirA complex (5 s) with the FGF2 translocation time (200 ms).

claim: No other cell surface HSPGs were found in proximity to FGF2 in the BioID screen.
source: Second, no other cell surface HSPGs were found in proximity to FGF2.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the BioID screen results.

claim: GPC1 and GPC5 are the two glypican family members expressed in HeLa S3 cells.
source: Following the identification of GPC1 as a cell surface HSPGs in cellular proximity to FGF2 (Figure 1), we engineered cell lines with knockouts of GPC1 and GPC5, the two family members expressed in HeLa S3 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A double knockout of GPC1 and GPC5 does not further intensify the FGF2 secretion phenotype observed in GPC1 knockout cells.
source: Consistently, a double knockout of GPC1 and GPC5 did not further intensify the FGF2 secretion phenotype observed in cells in which only GPC1 was knocked out.
evidence: This is shown in the secretion assays in Figure 2.

claim: GPC1 has a stronger impact on FGF2 secretion when the amounts of FGF2-GFP being expressed are limiting.
source: These findings suggest that GPC1 has an even stronger impact on this process when the amounts of FGF2-GFP being expressed are limiting.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the effect of GPC1 overexpression is more pronounced at low FGF2-GFP expression levels (Figure 5D).

claim: Individual GPC1-overexpressing cells showed more than 20-fold increase of FGF2-GFP particles on their cell surface compared to the average in wild-type cells.
source: Strikingly, individual cells were observed that were characterized by a more than 20-fold increase of FGF2-GFP particles on their cell surface compared to the average number of FGF2-GFP particles on the cell surfaces of wild-type cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the single molecule TIRF data in Figure 5D.

claim: The GPC family can be divided into two subclasses: GPC1/2/4/6 and GPC3/5.
source: Of note, the GPC family can be divided into two subclasses, GPC1/2/4/6 and GPC3/5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GPC classification.

claim: The spectrum of disaccharides from SDC4 shows features similar to GPC1 for disaccharide standards 1, 2, 6, and 12.
source: When the spectrum of disaccharides from GPC1 and GPC5 was compared with SDC4, most features were similar to GPC1 (disaccharide standards 1, 2, 6, and 12) while the abundance of the disaccharide corresponding to standard 5 was rather similar to GPC5 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the disaccharide composition analysis in Figure 7.

claim: The abundance of disaccharide standard 5 in SDC4 is similar to GPC5.
source: When the spectrum of disaccharides from GPC1 and GPC5 was compared with SDC4, most features were similar to GPC1 (disaccharide standards 1, 2, 6, and 12) while the abundance of the disaccharide corresponding to standard 5 was rather similar to GPC5 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the disaccharide composition analysis in Figure 7.

claim: FGF2 hexasaccharide binding sites are likely less abundant in GPC5 and SDC4 resulting in weaker interactions with FGF2.
source: Based on our findings, such binding sites are likely to be less abundant in GPC5 and SDC4 resulting in weaker interactions with FGF2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the disaccharide composition and binding data.

claim: The FGF2 binding sites in GPC1 stabilize the first subunits of membrane-spanning FGF2 oligomers as they surface at the outer plasma membrane leaflet.
source: Based upon the unique positioning of the heparan sulfate chains of GPC1 in close proximity to its GPI anchor and therefore the membrane surface (Prydz and Dalen, 2000; Blackhall et al., 2001; Nakato and Kimata, 2002; De Pasquale and Pavone, 2020), the FGF2 binding sites in GPC1 appear to be required for stabilizing the first subunits of membrane-spanning FGF2 oligomers as they surface at the outer plasma membrane leaflet.
evidence: This is proposed as a mechanism based on the structural properties of GPC1 and the secretion data.

claim: GPC1 overexpression increases the likelihood of membrane-spanning FGF2 oligomers to be formed.
source: In this way, the likeliness of these intermediates to be formed could be strongly increased when GPC1 is overexpressed.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the increased secretion efficiency with GPC1 overexpression.

claim: Higher forms of membrane-inserted FGF2 oligomers do not accumulate in cells lacking cell surface heparan sulfates.
source: These observations are consistent with previous findings demonstrating that, compared to wild-type cells, higher forms of membrane-inserted FGF2 oligomers do not accumulate in cells lacking cell surface heparan sulfates (Dimou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Dimou et al., 2019.
